article_title: Early Literacy and Learning Model/Plus (ELLM/Plus)
citation: Early Literacy and Learning Model (ELLM/Plus). (2008). Evidence rating summary, Preschool Curriculum Evaluation Research (PCER) studies.
title: ELLM coaching cycle: coach models a lesson, teacher implements it, and written analysis of critical behaviors feeds a feedback and reflection conference
description: The ELLM coaching cycle addresses effective teaching skills for each literacy component and runs from coach modeling to the teacher assimilating critical behaviors into daily practice. The coach first models a lesson demonstrating desired instructional behaviors while the teacher conducts a written analysis; a feedback and reflection conference asks "What worked? What needs to be added? What needs to be extended?". In the next cycle the teacher implements the lesson while the coach observes and analyzes the teacher's critical behaviors, followed by another conference in which coach and teacher plan the next cycle. Critical behaviors are specified in advance and analyzed during delivery.
requirements: Literacy coaches trained via a five-day summer institute and weekly coaching seminars
Critical behaviors specified in advance and analyzed during delivery
constraints: Additional support beyond the cycle is delivered only through abbreviated coaching sessions, teacher observations, or instructional materials
target_learners: Preschool teachers
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching skills and behaviors for each literacy component
examples: The first phase has the coach modeling the lesson while the teacher observes and conducts a written analysis
key_sources: Early Literacy and Learning Model (ELLM/Plus). (2008). Evidence rating summary, Preschool Curriculum Evaluation Research (PCER) studies. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/early-literacy-and-learning-model-plus-ellm-plus/
grain_size: lesson-level coaching cycle repeated across literacy components

article_title: Early Learning in Mathematics
citation: Early Learning in Mathematics (ELM): Evidence Rating. (2021). https://www.evidenceforessessments.org/early-learning-in-mathematics/
title: Focused coverage of a small number of key mathematical ideas with explicit, systematic instruction
description: ELM's instructional design pattern emphasizes depth over breadth: "The curriculum emphasizes a small number of key ideas in math to provide more focused coverage, instead of trying to teach a comprehensive but more surface set of skills." It pairs this focused coverage with "Explicit and systematic instructional design." The pattern structures a full year of 120 45-minute lessons plus daily calendar activities.
requirements: A full year of structured lessons (120 45-minute lessons plus daily 15-minute calendar activities) delivered by the classroom teacher.
constraints: The review does not isolate which design feature produced the effects; the pattern is described, not experimentally decomposed.
target_learners: kindergartners
target_learning_goals: core early mathematics concepts and skills
examples: ELM implements this pattern through 120 45-minute lessons and daily 15-minute calendar activities for the whole class.
key_sources: Early Learning in Mathematics (ELM): Evidence Rating. (2021). https://www.evidenceforessessments.org/early-learning-in-mathematics/

article_title: How Do Principals Influence Student Achievement?
citation: Elaine Allensworth. (2019). Elementary School Case Studies. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/how-do-principals-influence-student-achievement
title: Distributed leadership with monitoring routines in elementary schools
description: A school-level organizational pattern in which principals delegate leadership functions to staff (coaches, counselors, teachers) while maintaining regular instructional monitoring routines such as progress-report reviews, assignment feedback, and team data meetings. Both case schools distribute work among staff: at Foxglove the principal's philosophy is "putting the right people in the right place", and at Ivy the principal empowers staff to set goals. The cases suggest distribution works best paired with coordination and shared monitoring structures.
requirements: Staff members with capacity to own delegated functions, as at Ivy where the principal cites a strong staff
constraints: Foxglove's distributed model operated with few mechanisms to coordinate work within and across groups, and teachers reported limited scheduled collaboration time
target_learners: Elementary school students
target_learning_goals: School-wide academic achievement, growth targets, and student support
examples: Foxglove delegates discipline, finances, lesson-plan checking, attendance supports, and hiring; Ivy's grade-level teams create academic goals that the whole school reviews.

article_title: English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students
citation: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Franklin, K., Angeles, C., & Allensworth, E.M. (2024). English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Subgroup taxonomy of English Learners by classification history and disability status
description: The report organizes English Learners in high school into a taxonomy that disaggregates the broad active English Learner category into subgroups with distinct needs. Former English Learners "demonstrated English proficiency and exited EL status by the ninth grade"; long-term English Learners (with or without IEPs) had been in CPS six or more years without demonstrating proficiency on the ACCESS test; and late-arriving English Learners had been in CPS fewer than six years. The authors make this distinction because "the different experiences and needs of these subgroups are often not recognized" when districts report active English Learners as a whole. The taxonomy underpins every finding in the report.
requirements: Longitudinal administrative data on English Learner classification status, ACCESS test results, and IEP status at ninth-grade entry
constraints: Classification was based on student status at the beginning of ninth grade; a small group (2%) identified with a disability later remained in the without-IEP group
target_learners: High school English Learners in large urban districts
target_learning_goals: High school graduation and college access and persistence
examples: The report applied the taxonomy to 78,507 CPS students: 23% former, 4% long-term without IEP, 3% long-term with IEP, and 3% late-arriving English Learners

article_title: Family Playbook: How Can We Understand Students' Progress in School?
citation: UChicago Consortium on School Research. (2024). Family playbook: How can we understand students' progress in school? Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/events-and-resources
title: Elementary On-Track categories combine GPA and attendance thresholds into four support tiers
description: The playbook presents CPS's Elementary On-Track framework, introduced in 2018 to organize on-track work for younger students. It crosses two thresholds—GPA 3.0 and attendance 90%—yielding four categories: "On-Track: GPA 3.0+, Attendance 90%+"; Academic Support (GPA below 3.0, attendance 90%+); Attendance Support (GPA 3.0+, attendance below 90%); and Intensive Support (both below). Educators use the categories to ask who needs support, what students are experiencing, and whether strategies are working.
requirements: School-level GPA and attendance data to classify students into the four categories
constraints: Applied to students in grades 3-8 in Chicago Public Schools
target_learners: Elementary and middle school students (grades 3-8)
target_learning_goals: Monitoring academic progress and attendance to keep students on track for graduation
examples: CPS introduced the Elementary On-Track framework in 2018; the playbook's Data Dive shows category distributions for 6th-8th graders across SY14-SY22.

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners supports students to develop a sense of agency, confidence, and determination
description: The brief frames student agency as a core feature of quality instruction for English learners, defining it as the capacity and propensity to take purposeful initiative and noting that agency embraces self-regulated learning. It argues that language is a key resource for learning self-regulation, so teachers should design instruction that builds language and regulation in tandem, with cycles of goal setting, reflection, and revision.
requirements: Students and teachers need time, support, learning opportunities, and grace as they begin to integrate opportunities to develop self-regulation and agency.
target_learners: English learners (multilingual learners) in K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, agency, and English language development
examples: The brief suggests students begin by formulating a simple goal such as adding time order words to their writing, then over time define goals with a greater variety of language, supported by sentence frames like "When I first wrote the text, I thought…" "Now I think…".

article_title: The Effects of the Elevate Math Summer Program on Math Achievement and Algebra Readiness
citation: Snipes, J., Huang, C.-W., Jaquet, K., & Finkelstein, N. (2016). The effects of the Elevate Math summer program on math achievement and algebra readiness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: Elevate Math summer program
description: Elevate Math is a math support program by the Silicon Valley Education Foundation whose core is "an intensive 75-hour (19 days over four weeks) summer preparatory course" for rising grade 8 students. It has four components: a Common Core–based curriculum with four content modules; about 19 days of four hours of blended instruction with one daily hour on Khan Academy; a college field trip and family college information night; and 40 hours of Common Core–based professional development for teachers and teacher assistants.
requirements: Credentialed teachers and college-level teacher assistants who receive the 40 hours of Common Core State Standards–based professional development
constraints: The study reports the program is not sufficient by itself for ensuring students are ready for challenging middle school math courses

algebra readiness

article_title: National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report: Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress
citation: Cook, G., Linquanti, R., Chinen, M., & Jung, H. (2012). National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report—Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress. American Institutes for Research, Washington, DC. http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/index.html
title: Three accountability methods for taking ELs' ELP level into account when setting academic progress and proficiency expectations: progressive benchmarking, indexed progress, and status-and-growth accountability matrix
description: Chapter IV presents an organizing framework of methods for setting academic expectations for English Learners. "Progressive benchmarking methods are illustrated that adjust either EL students' content achievement scale scores or their weight (individual 'count'), based on each student's ELP level relative to their initial ELP level and time in the state school system." An indexed progress method uses ELs' ELP growth as a weighted, time-sensitive proxy for English language arts performance for newly arrived ELs entering at lower initial ELP levels. A status and growth accountability matrix method credits predetermined academic growth and proficiency attainment without considering ELP level.
requirements: Application requires student-level longitudinal data linking ELP assessments, content assessments, time in the state school system, and initial ELP level
constraints: The report notes the SGAM method explicitly ignores the EL's ELP level, contrasting with the two adjustment methods; each method is applied to one education agency's sample data set
target_learners: English Learners, particularly newly arrived ELs entering at lower initial ELP levels, in grade 3 and similar grades
target_learning_goals: Academic progress and proficiency expectations in English language arts and mathematics accountability systems
examples: All three methods were applied using the same education agency's sample data set (Education Agency 1, grade 3, N = 18,101 ELs in outcome comparisons)

article_title: Successful Teacher Residencies: What Matters and What Works
citation: Yun, C., & Fitz, J. (2025). Successful teacher residencies: What matters and what works. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/480.783
title: Eleven characteristics of high-quality teacher residencies: eight research-based characteristics plus three emerging from the case studies
description: Across the five case study programs, eleven practices emerged as promoters of success. Eight align with characteristics previously identified by the Learning Policy Institute and Pathways Alliance: strong LEA–EPP partnerships; selectively recruited diverse candidates; a full-year teaching experience alongside an expert mentor teacher; expert mentor teachers who coteach; tightly integrated coursework and clinical practice; cohorts of residents; financial supports for residents; and ongoing mentoring and support for graduates. Three additional characteristics emerged from the current study: "Proactive whole person supports that residents can easily access through a 'go-to person,'" ongoing program capacity development, and an explicit focus on promoting equity for residents and their students.
requirements: Programs must implement the characteristics in context-specific ways that fit partner LEA needs and available funding
constraints: The report notes that because programs drew on different funding sources, not all practices discussed aligned with TRGP requirements
target_learners: Teacher residents in postbaccalaureate residency pathways
target_learning_goals: High-quality preparation for teaching in high-need shortage areas
Equity-focused teaching practices
examples: Case study programs served between 15 and 325 residents, offered hybrid, online, and in-person formats, and ranged from 10 to 18 months in length

citation: Haycock, Kati. (1998). Good Teaching Matters: How Well-Qualified Teachers Can Close the Gap. Thinking K-16, v3 n2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED457260
title: El Paso Collaborative for Academic Excellence
description: A comprehensive effort created in 1992 by the University of Texas-El Paso and the three El Paso-area school districts (El Paso, Ysleta, and Socorro) to raise student achievement kindergarten through college. Its goal was to prepare every young person in the city to enter college without remediation, reflected in the El Paso Standards. Teachers received intensive assistance including summer institutes and regular on-site coaching, funded through NSF dollars and redirected federal and state funds, while the University changed teacher preparation. The article reports improved achievement and a narrower gap between ethnic groups on TAAS math passing rates from 1992-93 to 1997-98.

constraints: The district context is described as a highly impoverished border city

Predominantly Hispanic and low-income students
Prospective teachers at UTEP
target_learning_goals: College entry without remediation
Improved mathematics achievement across ethnic groups

citation: Losen, D. J., & Martinez, P. (2020). Lost opportunities: How disparate school discipline continues to drive differences in the opportunity to learn. Learning Policy Institute; Center for Civil Rights Remedies at the Civil Rights Project, UCLA. http://www.schooldisciplinedata.org
title: Eliminate out-of-school suspensions for minor misconduct and replace punitive exclusion with supportive, educational alternatives
description: The report recommends that policymakers eliminate out-of-school suspensions and expulsions for lower-level offenses and reduce suspension length for other offenses, replacing punitive discipline with responses that serve an educational purpose. It urges educators to "pursue nonpunitive strategies—alternatives that teach responsibility, enhance social and emotional learning, and help students improve their conduct," including trauma-informed, restorative, and culturally responsive practices, supported by teacher training in classroom management.

article_title: Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions
citation: Li Siyan, Kai-Hui Liang, Shopnil Shahriar, Yilin Ye, Shiyoh Goetsu, Wei-Wei Du, Masahiro Yoshida, Tsunayuki Ohwa, Xuhai Xu, and Zhou Yu. (2026). Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641
title: Elaboration Likelihood Model peripheral-route account of empathy's invisible impact
description: The article interprets its pattern of results — empathy's effects appearing in behavioral trajectories rather than in users' explicit ratings — through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route. The authors state: "We interpret this pattern through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route." On this account, empathy acts as a peripheral cue that shapes motivation and trust supporting sustained change, even when "it may be hard for lay users to identify explicitly". This framing explains why perceived-empathy ratings diverge from measured outcomes in their study.
requirements: A multi-session coaching context in which users repeatedly interact with the chatbot over time
Outcome measures that capture behavioral trajectories (e.g., step counts, intention over days) rather than only single-shot perception ratings
constraints: The article offers this as an interpretation of its observed pattern, not as a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: Inactive but motivated adults using digital PA coaching tools
target_learning_goals: Motivation and adherence in physical activity behavior change
Trust in and rapport with a coaching chatbot
examples: The authors use this account to explain why the Empathetic chatbot improved intention and self-efficacy faster while participants could not consciously distinguish the versions

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: ELEVATE: a three-stratum framework for locally deployed GenAI avatar tutors
description: ELEVATE (Efficient LLM Education with Virtual Avatar Teaching Engine) is a framework for developing GenAI-driven avatar tutors governed by institutional epistemic infrastructures. It integrates "LLM-driven dialogue with embodied 3D avatars for multimodal interaction" and adopts a local-first execution model. The framework "formalizes a three-stratum design that separates (i) a student-facing virtual avatar interaction layer, (ii) a local GenAI execution and multimodal synthesis core, and (iii) a teacher-facing governance layer", forming a closed loop in which teacher-defined constraints govern engine behavior and the avatar embodies responses.
requirements: Deployment on local or on-premise institutional hardware without cloud dependency
Teacher-defined constraints encoded as system-level specifications governing LLM and retrieval behavior
constraints: The authors adopt a system-level perspective and do not aim to evaluate learning outcomes directly
target_learners: school students across heterogeneous educational levels and subjects
target_learning_goals: personalized tutoring and real-time question answering aligned with curriculum requirements
examples: A working prototype was implemented and deployed in a real-world educational curriculum aligned with curriculum requirements, running on standard PCs and smartphones
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: ELEVATE Engine: streaming, queue-based client-server pipeline for low perceived latency
description: The ELEVATE Engine is the framework's technical core, split into a client that renders the avatar and manages interaction and a server that performs LLM inference and speech synthesis. Its central design choice is streaming generation: "Instead of waiting for a full response completion, the server emits partial outputs (e.g., paragraphs or chunks) as soon as they are available." Queue-based orchestration decouples ASR, LLM, and TTS stages so generation proceeds independently of synthesis, avoiding cascaded blocking and supporting incremental delivery with per-segment ordering metadata.
requirements: Explicit client-side coordination for ordering, validation/decryption, and audiovisual synchronization of streamed segments
Queue-based orchestration between pipeline modules
constraints: The reference implementation's interaction boundary is text-based: speech-to-text runs on the client device and the server receives only textual prompts, with no server-side ASR module
target_learners: school students interacting via smartphones, desktop PCs, and immersive 3D environments
target_learning_goals: responsive conversational tutoring with timely feedback and smooth turn-taking
examples: The server pipeline can be horizontally partitioned across multiple low-end consumer nodes, with Orchestrator, LLM inference, and TTS running as separate processes communicating through the same message interface

citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Teacher Interaction Layer: a web-based configuration surface for pedagogical intent, persona, and role
description: The Teacher Interaction Layer is a lightweight web-based configuration page through which educators shape the virtual tutor's behavior; all settings are injected directly into the LLM system prompt. It exposes personality presets (e.g., Neutral, Friendly, Patient, Verbose, Concise, plus a Custom option), thumbnail-based avatar appearance selection, a knowledge base selector, and teacher type. "The interface specifies the type of teacher through mutually exclusive radio-button options (e.g., professor (replicating lecture content), tutor (providing repeated explanations and scaffolding), and exam trainer", with a save action persisting settings as reproducible configuration artifacts.
requirements: Settings must be persisted as configuration artifacts (templates, rule sets, corpus descriptors) interpreted by the server at runtime for traceability
constraints: Personality presets are deliberately constrained; styles beyond them require additional engineering inputs such as tailored prompt templates or policy rules
target_learners: students in classrooms configured by their teachers
target_learning_goals: consistent, pedagogically framed tutoring behavior matching classroom norms and assessment contexts
examples: Thumbnail-based avatar selection was chosen to keep configuration concrete and low-effort while avoiding value-laden textual descriptors, supporting a gender-respectful workflow

citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Five-stage game-ready asset production pipeline for a pedagogically controlled 3D Virtual Teacher avatar
description: The prototype's Virtual Teacher avatar was manually authored rather than sourced from a pre-packaged library, to give pedagogical control over appearance and expressive affordances. The pipeline runs through Character Creator, ZBrush sculpt refinement, Substance Painter material authoring, Mixamo auto-rigging and animation, and OBJ export. The authors treat the avatar as part of the interaction channel, in which "facial expressions, turn-taking cues, and lip synchronization are treated as communicative signals that shape how students interpret the tutor's epistemic stance and instructional intent".
requirements: Face mesh must support clear lip articulation to avoid degrading comprehension during voice-based tutoring
Polygon count, texture sizes, and shader complexity must keep the asset computationally tractable on consumer hardware for stable frame rates under concurrency
constraints: Texture resolution was balanced to preserve facial readability while limiting VRAM and bandwidth overhead for mobile and consumer devices
target_learners: school students interacting with the avatar on smartphones and PCs
target_learning_goals: legible embodied communication of tutor state and instructional intent
examples: Mixamo was used to obtain baseline idle and conversational animations, enabling rapid iteration on embodied behaviors without bespoke animation production

article_title: ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models
citation: Yilin Jiang, Xiaorong Zhu, Fei Tan, Zicheng Zhang, Kaiyi Huang, Yang Yu, Zexuan Fei, Yiming Luo, Keqian Li, Hao Hao, Guangtao Zhai, Aimin Zhou. (2026). ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09548
title: ELBench: a four-module benchmark of 2939 items for education-facing LLMs with task-appropriate scoring
description: ELBench evaluates education-facing large language models under a common protocol across four modules totaling 2939 items: General Capability (894 curated items), Safety and Trustworthiness (1000 self-built plus curated items), Basic Education (45 items curated from ELMES), and High-Level Cultivation (1000 self-built items). Closed-form tasks use "reference matching or deterministic task-specific checks", while open-ended tasks are scored by rubric-based LLM judging with Qwen3.6 as judge (mean κ of 0.83) and majority vote over N = 9 calls. Item scores are normalized to a 0–100 scale per module, and the overall score is the unweighted mean of the four module scores.
requirements: Open-ended scoring depends on a rubric-based LLM judge selected for agreement with expert human annotation, with majority voting over N = 9 calls and randomized presentation order to control position bias
constraints: The self-built data is expert-verified but synthetic, and the benchmark is text-only
The model set is a sample of nine representative systems, so group-level claims describe this set
The safety module measures behavior against one education-oriented specification that includes region-specific content
Module sizes are uneven by design
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education learners served by education-facing LLM tutors and teaching assistants
target_learning_goals: Accurate knowledge and reasoning
Safe behavior under sensitive prompts
Production of usable instructional material
Pedagogical judgment aligned with learner development

article_title: Relations between the worked example and generation effects on immediate and delayed tests
citation: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016.
title: Element interactivity as the cognitive load theory measure reconciling the worked example and generation effects
description: Within cognitive load theory, element interactivity is the measure of material complexity: "Interactive elements are defined as elements that must be processed simultaneously in working memory in order to complete a task". It determines intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load and varies with learner expertise, since experts retrieve interacting elements from long-term memory as single units. The article uses it to resolve the contradiction between the worked example effect (guidance helps) and the generation effect (generation helps): the worked example effect "relies on high element interactivity material while the generation effect relies on low element interactivity material", with expertise reducing effective element interactivity. Human cognitive architecture is described via five principles, including the information store, borrowing and reorganizing, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, and environmental organizing and linking principles.
requirements: Applying the measure requires counting interacting elements for the specific learners, since expertise changes the effective count.
constraints: The article scopes its claims to acquisition of domain-specific schemas in long-term memory, citing Kalyuga and Singh (2015) that cognitive load theory may not apply to goals such as motivating learners or acquiring generalized schemas for transfer.
target_learners: Novice and more expert learners of curriculum-based problem-solving and memorization tasks
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of domain-specific schemas in long-term memory
examples: Estimating about 71 interacting elements in a trigonometry simplification task for Year 10 novices versus a count of one for formula memorization

description: The article explains its findings through two learning principles. article_title: Elementary tests in psychology.
citation: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Elemental tests: the distinction between psycho-physic sensibility and the apperceptive use of a sense
description: Seashore proposes that a test is "elemental" when it is so simple and direct that no improvement can be made in the record by training, and that the record of such a test should not vary with age or phenomenal use of the sense. The framework distinguishes inborn sensory capacity (physiological threshold) from acquired skill in using a sense (cognitive threshold). The Iowa laboratory sought verification through two lines of experiment: measurement of the effect of extraordinary use of a sense (the blind) and prolonged training on a presumably elemental test.
requirements: Tests must be reduced to simple, direct impressions reportable by the most natural response, with no skill in action involved, to approximate a physiological rather than a cognitive threshold.
constraints: No test can be made absolute, since even the most elemental test involves some general power of observation acquired by training; a child must be old enough to apply himself to the task.
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: measuring inborn sensory capacity distinct from trained skill
examples: The six measurements on blind and seeing pupils, and the thirteen-observer training study on intensity of sound, were designed as verifications of this principle.

description: The review concludes that e‐learning should be combined with traditional instructional methods rather than used alone. It states that "E‐learning is a complementary tool rather than a stand‐alone solution, and is most effective alongside traditional face‐to‐face teaching." The flipped‐classroom model is cited as an exemplar strategy, enabling learners to acquire foundational knowledge through e‐learning before face‐to‐face sessions focused on higher‐order cognitive skills, allowing efficient use of limited curriculum time during ENT clinical placements.

constraints: Skill development via e‐learning alone is limited; the review notes technical barriers and the impersonal nature of e‐learning as detracting factors

clinical skills development

article_title: Acute effect of physical activity on academic outcomes in school-aged youth: A systematic review and multivariate meta-analysis.
citation: Muntaner-Mas A, Morales JS, Martínez-de-Quel Ó, Lubans DR, García-Hermoso A. (2024). Acute effect of physical activity on academic outcomes in school-aged youth: A systematic review and multivariate meta-analysis. Scand J Med Sci Sports. https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.14479
title: Active breaks as the predominant form of acute physical activity in the reviewed interventions
description: Active breaks were the predominant form of physical activity in the included studies (10 out of 11). The article characterizes them as interventions that take into account "neither the embodiment (physical activity is not related to a learning task) nor the integration (there is no temporal overlap between movements and the learning task) concepts". Despite lacking these features, the review's findings suggest that human movement with minimal cognitive load may still improve academic performance, and the authors argue active breaks are an appealing strategy for educational contexts because timing and planning are key barriers to movement-based interventions.
requirements: A single bout of physical activity delivered during the school day, separate from the learning task
constraints: Active breaks lack embodiment and integration with academic content, which the authors note as a limitation relative to embodied learning techniques
target_learners: School-aged children and adolescents in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Academic performance (mathematics, language) and classroom behavior
examples: Included interventions used active breaks of 4 to 30 minutes, with 20 minutes the most common bout duration, mostly applying acute aerobic exercise.

title: Kolb's experiential learning theory as the framework for designing concrete experiences with reflection and abstraction
description: The study is framed by Kolb's (1984) experiential learning theory, in which learners move through "a concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation". The article uses ELT to structure a biofuels lesson varying when the abstract lecture occurs relative to a concrete laboratory and whether reflection happens during or after the laboratory. Reflection is treated as "a mechanism for the construction of knowledge from experience". Roberts's four contextual dimensions (level, duration, intended outcome, setting) are also cited as requirements for experiential learning to occur.
requirements: All four stages of the cycle must be present for experiential learning; teachers need knowledge of the cycle to plan curricula
constraints: Prior research found experiential learning was implemented but not always cyclical in agriscience classrooms

target_learning_goals: content knowledge of biofuels
discussion skills
calculation skills
examples: The biofuels lesson compared energy stored in kerosene and ethanol via a Lab-Aids laboratory activity with lecture/discussion placed before or after the lab

citation: Andy Bown. (2017). Elaborative Feedback to Enhance Online Second Language Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p164
title: Elaborative feedback as sociocultural scaffolding for compensatory L2 reading processing
description: The article frames elaborative feedback as scaffolding, defined as the "process of supportive dialogue which directs the attention of the learner to key features of the environment". Drawing on Bernhardt's Compensatory Model and McNeil's extension, it argues that feedback enhances comprehension only when it supplies additional knowledge the reader can use for compensatory processing when a difficulty is encountered, and that this need varies with proficiency level.
requirements: Feedback should be carefully targeted at the needs of learners working within their zone of proximal development
constraints: The same feedback that supports lower-proficiency readers may not correspond to the needs of higher-proficiency readers
target_learners: higher education L2 English readers
target_learning_goals: online L2 reading comprehension
examples: The study's elaborative feedback version guided readers with prompts such as re-reading a paragraph and comparing menu types, while the knowledge of response version stated only Incorrect.

title: Experiential Learning Care (ELC) model: King's Theory of Goal Attainment integrated with Kolb-style experiential learning stages
description: ELC is a nursing intervention model in which the transaction between nurse and mother required by King's Theory of Goal Attainment is operationalized as structured experiential learning. The article states "Researchers found King's theory would be appropriate if it is integrated with the Experiential Learning", using experience as a catalyst so mothers learn preterm care by doing. Its four stages are printed as "1) Phase practice of concrete (Concrete Experience) 2) Phase Active and Reflective Experience (Reflection Observation). 3) Conceptualization Phase (Abstract Conceptualization). 4) Phase Experimentation Active (Active Experimentation)." The ELC module structures mothers' experience from problem awareness through observing nurses to demonstrating mastered skills.
requirements: Nurses and midwives act as facilitators of the mother's active involvement in every element of ELC, per the article's implementation factors
constraints: The article notes King's theory alone was abstract at the transactional stage and could not immediately be applied concretely, motivating the ELC integration
target_learners: mothers of preterm infants hospitalized in perinatal wards
target_learning_goals: independent preterm infant care skills after hospital discharge
recognizing signs of apnea, hypothermia, impaired nutrition and infection
examples: In phase 2, mothers received the ELC module for 2 weeks from the first day of birth, and independence was observed after discharge up to 28 days from birth

article_title: A Quasi-Experimental Examination: Cognitive Sequencing of Instruction Using Experiential Learning Theory for STEM Concepts in Agricultural Education
citation: Kasee L. Smith & John Rayfield. (2017). A Quasi-Experimental Examination: Cognitive Sequencing of Instruction Using Experiential Learning Theory for STEM Concepts in Agricultural Education. Journal of Agricultural Education, 58(4), 175-191. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2017.04175
title: Kolb's experiential learning theory as a framework for cognitive sequencing of instruction
description: The study's conceptual framework combines Kolb's experiential learning theory with Gagne's nine events of instruction. ELT models learning as "the cyclical process of the experiential learning cycle" with four modes — active experimentation, concrete experience, reflective observation, and abstract conceptualization — organized into two dialectically opposed pairs, with grasping experience occurring through apprehension (concrete experience) or comprehension (abstract conceptualization). The study used this framework to manipulate only the cognitive sequence of the "presenting the stimulus" event while holding the other instructional events constant.
requirements: The entire learning cycle must be completed in order for learning to occur, with the concrete experience supplemented by reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation
constraints: The study examined only the grasping dimension of ELT, not the transformation dimension
Gagne's nine events of instruction were held constant except for presenting the stimulus
target_learners: secondary students in introductory agricultural science courses
target_learning_goals: abstract STEM concepts in water and soil science
examples: Two units of experimental curricula were each developed in two formats: one beginning each new concept with a concrete experience moving toward abstract conceptualization, and the other in the opposite sequence

citation: Rohollahzadeh Ebadi, M., Mohd Saad, M. R., & Abedalaziz, N. (2013). Explicit Form Focus Instruction: The Effects on Implicit and Explicit Knowledge of ESL Learners. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(4). https://www.moj-es.net
title: Four-test battery separately measuring implicit and explicit L2 knowledge (EOIT, TGJT, UGJT, MKT)
description: The study used four adapted instruments (from Bowles, 2011; Ellis et al., 2009) to measure the two knowledge types separately: the Elicited Oral Imitation Test (EOIT) and Timed Grammaticality Judgment Test (TGJT) for implicit knowledge, and the Untimed Grammaticality Judgment Test (UGJT) and Metalinguistic Knowledge Test (MKT) for explicit knowledge. The article states these tests were chosen because they "incorporat[e] the distinguishing criteria of the two types of language knowledge within their design". Explicit knowledge was scored using UGJT ungrammatical items, which prior research indicated provide a stronger measure of explicit knowledge.
requirements: Tests must incorporate the distinguishing criteria of implicit and explicit knowledge in their design; a pilot showed Cronbach's alpha reliability values above .80 for all four tests
constraints: The article notes "The main limitation of the research to date lies in the method of testing" and calls its conclusions provisional based on the available tests
target_learners: adult lower-intermediate ESL learners
target_learning_goals: separate measurement of implicit and explicit grammatical knowledge
examples: The EOIT was administered individually with audio-recorded oral reproduction of sentences; the TGJT, UGJT and MKT were completed in a single session of approximately 1.5 hours.

title: Eleven tree-thinking skills framework for phylogenetics competence
description: The article organizes phylogenetics competence as a set of eleven tree-thinking skills, seven of which were collectively described by Novick and Catley (2013). constraints: The program was developed within the framework of the existing syllabus for low-achieving eighth graders

Each student completed "12 standardized VSP cases" representing common internal medicine scenarios, with "up to 3 attempts per case" and immediate feedback after each attempt. Its intelligent module scored consultation skills, diagnostic accuracy, treatment planning, and overall clinical reasoning.
requirements: All teachers supervising VSP sessions completed a standardized 8-hour training program covering technical operation, facilitation, feedback, and troubleshooting, and passed a competency assessment before supervising sessions
Teachers provide guidance and training on software usage methods for students, who work in small groups of 10
constraints: The VSP system primarily focuses on textbook-style disease presentations, potentially neglecting case variations and atypical scenarios encountered in real clinical practice
The predefined decision-tree branches may restrict students' exploration of alternative diagnostic hypotheses, limiting the simulation's flexibility
target_learners: fifth-year undergraduate medical students interning at Quzhou People's Hospital
target_learning_goals: clinical thinking ability
history taking, examination selection, diagnosis, and treatment planning
examples: VSP scoring was cross-validated against blinded expert evaluations by 3 senior clinicians who reviewed 20% of randomly selected VSP sessions; interrater reliability (Fleiss κ=0.81) confirmed consistency between automated and manual scoring
The system's test covered 4 components: medical interview (25 points), condition examination (30 points), diagnosis and differential (25 points), and treatment plan (20 points)

article_title: An osteoporosis course as a separate component of problem-based learning.
citation: Hoffmanová I, Džupa V, Waldauf P, Grill R, Báča V. (2025). An osteoporosis course as a separate component of problem-based learning. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0336915
title: Elective Osteoporosis Course: blended e-learning plus PBL case seminars consolidating content dispersed across five mandatory courses
description: A two-part elective for fourth-year medical students consolidating osteoporosis content otherwise spread across five mandatory courses. Each sub-course comprised "14 study hours, combining 10 hours of self-directed e-learning via an online platform" with two interactive 2-hour PBL seminars built on clinical cases. Students prepared a assigned case topic, presented reasoning, and received faculty feedback; assessment used a scaled multiple-choice test with a 70% passing threshold. More than 250 students completed the course over its 12 years of existence.

An e-learning platform providing a structured knowledge framework before the seminars
Faculty who guide the case debate and provide feedback aligned with established clinical practice
constraints: The course consolidates existing mandatory-course content without introducing new material
Elective status was chosen because mandatory integration into the existing curriculum was not feasible

target_learning_goals: osteoporosis pathophysiology, diagnostics, and pharmacological treatment
treatment of osteoporotic fractures and rehabilitation
clinical reasoning and collaborative problem-solving
examples: In each seminar, five cases were discussed, resulting in a total of ten clinical cases per sub-course

article_title: A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Aboueisha Hadeel, Abouzeid Enjy, Sallam Moataz A., Talaat Wagdy. (2025). A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08005-w
title: Four-part e-LbC case structure with breakout-room peer discussion and expert feedback
description: The e-LbC sessions in this study followed a recurring case structure combining ambiguous clinical presentations with peer discussion and expert feedback. The article describes the final structure of each case as: "(1) an initial ambiguous presentation, (2) a list of student-generated hypotheses, (3) new 'what-if' clinical information, and (4) a reflection and justification segment." Students worked in breakout rooms of 5–7 on Microsoft Teams to formulate diagnostic hypotheses and judge the effect of new information, then returned to the large group where the content expert reviewed answers, probed rationales, and gave feedback from the experts. The structure was repeated for investigative and treatment purposes.
requirements: A content expert leads the session and a faculty instructor monitors breakout rooms; the breakout-room function of the conferencing platform is needed to divide students into small groups
constraints: The article notes designing LbC cases presents the challenge of creating clinical scenarios that guide students in developing reasoning for complex and uncertain situations
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clerkship
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning under diagnostic uncertainty
formulating and revising diagnostic hypotheses
examples: Sessions on painless vision loss conditions such as central retinal vein occlusion, retinal detachment, optic neuritis, and ischemic ON followed this four-part structure over a 2-hour session

title: 3D-Printed Arthroscopic Shoulder Simulator (3DP)

Senior medical students

Shoulder anatomy knowledge

article_title: Enhancing radiographic interpretation: effects of gamification on medical students' knowledge, skills, and satisfaction - a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Karimian Z, Momeni M, Zarifsanaiey N. (2025). Enhancing radiographic interpretation: effects of gamification on medical students' knowledge, skills, and satisfaction — a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07523-x
title: Experiential Learning Theory and Self-Determination Theory as the theoretical basis for gamification in medical education
description: The article grounds gamification in two frameworks. Experiential Learning Theory (Kolb) holds that "learning is most effective when it is an active, cyclical process involving four stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation", which gamified interactive activities mirroring real-world challenges are said to support. Self-Determination Theory adds that fulfilling needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness fosters intrinsic motivation, and gamification elements such as goal setting, learner control, and feedback can be designed to support these needs.
requirements: Gamification elements must be purposefully designed to support autonomy (choice of learning paths), competence (opportunities to demonstrate mastery), and relatedness (collaboration)
constraints: The frameworks are presented as theoretical support; the study itself does not test the mechanisms directly
target_learners: medical students in gamified learning environments
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation, engagement, and deeper learning and retention
examples: The gamified platform operationalized competence through levels and mastery thresholds and feedback through color-coded correctness responses
key_sources: Karimian Z, Momeni M, Zarifsanaiey N. (2025). Enhancing radiographic interpretation: effects of gamification on medical students' knowledge, skills, and satisfaction — a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07523-x

title: Support e-learning implementation in low-connectivity settings with offline module access, local assistance and a technical helpdesk
description: The article recommends designing e-learning for LMIC rural contexts around known barriers (computer literacy, internet access, bandwidth). "A helpdesk to assist learners overcome the technical issues they might encounter is key to a smooth implementation of an e‐learning program." Offline access lets learners "study at any time and at their own pace, without having to rely on internet connectivity", and local support via phone for learners new to e-learning helped overcome barriers in isolated areas of Mali.

citation: Recker F, Neubauer R, Dong Y, Gschmack AM, Jenssen C, Möller K, Blaivas M, Ignacio Prats M, Lucius C, Ruppert J, Sänger SL, Sirli R, Weimer J, Westerway SC, Zervides C, Dietrich CF. (2024). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06092-9
title: Nicholls et al.'s eleven-step skills teaching model for complex psychomotor ultrasound skills
description: The review describes an evidenced-based instructional approach for teaching complex psychomotor skills, in which large multi-dimensional skills are broken down into sub-sets taught individually and "gradually reconstructed until whole task practice is achieved and performed". The model's eleven steps run from task analysis (no more than 7 to 9 sequenced steps) through pre-skill conceptualization, silent and verbalized demonstration, verbalization-execution, guided performance with withheld feedback, narrated practice with immediate error correction, short practice sessions under 60 minutes, to post-skill-execution feedback. It is presented as avoiding cognitive overload when multi-dimensional skills are taught in a single session.
requirements: A tutor who knows the topic well, has communication skills, and provides feedback, in a supportive learning environment
constraints: Complex skills cannot usually be taught in a single teaching session and must be broken into sub-units
target_learners: medical students learning ultrasound scanning skills
target_learning_goals: psychomotor ultrasound skills such as image acquisition and optimization
examples: The review's example of teaching aorta scanning and measuring is decomposed into a survey scan in sagittal and transverse planes, adjusting depth, focus and gain, image optimisation, and accurate caliper placement

title: Experiential learning theory (ELT) four-stage cycle as the organizing framework for patient eHealth education

The article divides the program into "4 stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation": concrete experience introduces eHealth care through real-life examples and scenarios; reflective observation uses videos, group discussions, and session reviews; abstract conceptualization clarifies eHealth concepts using social media platforms such as LINE and Facebook; and active experimentation has patients choose suitable health technology in a simulation environment and set self-management goals. The program was also based on the eHealth literacy framework (eHLF).
requirements: Activities must closely resemble patients' real-life situations and daily self-management tasks
constraints: Applied here to adult patients with type 2 diabetes in a clinical case-management context in Taiwan
target_learners: Adult patients with chronic disease learning to use eHealth technology
target_learning_goals: eHealth literacy
self-management skills
willingness to use health technology
examples: In the active experimentation stage, patients participated in group and individual competitions using eHealth care tools and were encouraged to use eHealth activities at home

article_title: The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition.
citation: Lebert, A., & Vilarroya, Ó. (2024). The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition. Ann NY Acad Sci, 1541, 37–52. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.15238
title: Experiential learning as a cycle of concrete experience, reflection, conceptualization, and application
description: Experiential learning is presented as a pedagogical approach viewing learning as "a continuous cycle of experience, reflection, and application", summarized as experience + reflection + new application = learning. Kolb's model is described as a four-stage cycle in which "information is received through concrete experience and abstract conceptualization and subsequently processed through reflective observation and active experimentation". EL was built on constructivism (Piaget, Vygotsky), introduced concrete experience as the source of learning, emphasized embodiment and situatedness, and produced implementable instructional practices. Individuals differ in their preferences for the four phases.
requirements: Hands-on experiences within a structured learning environment, typically guided by an educator, followed by reflection and application
constraints: The article notes that what exactly counts as a 'concrete experience' in the Kolb model remains unresolved
target_learners: learners across formal educational settings and real-world training contexts
target_learning_goals: skill acquisition and knowledge development through experience, reflection, and application
examples: Historically applied in 1940s intergroup-conflict initiatives, 1950s–60s humanistic and business training, and academic psychology from the 1970s onward.

title: Use contemporary e-learning rather than written course material for pre-course preparation in postgraduate medical courses
description: The article's results support preparing course participants with e-learning modules rather than self-study of written material: "Our results showed that the e‐learning prepared the participants better than the written course material." The authors attribute the advantage to e-learning's variety of teaching opportunities—interactive learning, case-based learning, multimedia and integrated tests highlighting knowledge gaps. constraints: The demonstrated mean difference of 1.8 points was smaller than the 10% (approximated 3 points) defined as educationally relevant; no advantage was found for anxiety, simulation performance, or 12-week retention
target_learners: resident anaesthetists in postgraduate specialty training
target_learning_goals: pre-course knowledge preparation for simulation-based courses
examples: In the RCT, all participants received e-learning in one subject and written national recommendations in the other before a two-day compulsory obstetric anaesthesia course

title: Elastic Grey Wolf Optimization (EGWO) algorithm
description: EGWO is a variant of the Grey Wolf Optimization swarm intelligence algorithm that the article proposes to remedy GWO's local stagnation and premature convergence. It adds three mechanisms: "the shrinking, resilient surrounding, and weighted candidate mechanisms are introduced to remedy the local stagnation and premature convergence deficiencies". The shrinking mechanism updates parameters A and C using Cauchy-distribution-inspired random values; the resilient surrounding mechanism changes how the α, β, and δ wolf positions are updated; and the weighted candidate mechanism generates candidate wolves so hunting is not limited to the α wolf.
requirements: Requires initialization of a wolf population and parameters a, A, and C, with a reduced linearly from 2 to 0 along with iterations
constraints: Proposed under No Free Lunch reasoning that no algorithm can effectively solve all problems; evaluated here only on MLP weight/bias optimization for student achievement prediction
target_learners: secondary school students (Mathematics and Portuguese subjects)
target_learning_goals: predicting student achievement from family features and personal characteristics
examples: Algorithm 2 sets the top three wolves as α, β and δ, updates their positions by Eqs (20)–(22), computes weights w1 to w3 by Eq (23), and generates candidate wolves by Eqs (24) to (27)

title: VolumetricOR virtual reality demonstrator for surgical workflow training
description: VolumetricOR is a virtual reality demonstrator that places users inside a photorealistic virtual operating room recorded at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, where they navigate sequences of a living kidney donation surgery. junior physicians
medical students and surgical staff
surgical assistants and nurses as recruitment candidates

team roles and decision-making paths in the operating room
spatial and instrument arrangement knowledge
examples: The team recorded a living donor kidney transplantation procedure at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin and integrated the volumetric video into a photogrammetric model of the operating room built with Metashape and Unreal Engine.

constraints: The mechanism account is the authors' interpretation; the trial measured anxiety outcomes, not the proposed conditioning or self-efficacy pathway directly

target_learning_goals: Reduced dental anxiety, familiarity with dental procedures, improved self-efficacy
